subtype: Approach: reflecting and reallocating after a missed milestone [Revision]
passage: Thursday night. First deadline missed today: the circuit board isn't wired. Feeling flat. Instead of blaming anyone, at lunch I sat with Divyansh and the others and asked why. Honest answers: I gave the wiring one afternoon and it needs three. The report looked small but takes an evening. We all guessed low for the hard parts and high for the easy ones. New plan: wiring gets three afternoons, Divyansh moves from decoration to help with wiring, the report gets two evenings shared between us. The teacher agreed to move the deadline by four days. Still tired, but not panicky. Small win: nobody was blamed, and everybody knows their share. - Sabina

qa.q: How many afternoons does the wiring now get?
qa.a: The wiring now gets three afternoons.

qa.q: How does Sabina feel at the end of the diary entry?
qa.a: Sabina feels tired but calmer and not panicky, and pleased that nobody was blamed.

qa.q: What could the team do to avoid missing the next deadline, and why?
qa.a: They could estimate the hard parts first and add extra time for them, because the missed deadline came from guessing low on the difficult tasks.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel about moving from decoration to wiring?
qa.a: Divyansh may feel a mix of challenge and importance, since the harder job matters more to the deadline.

grounding: When the first deadline is missed, the team looks at why, finds tasks were underestimated, and redistributes work with more time allowed for the harder parts.
